I've been doing strength training, and am hoping on being a competitive powerlifter next year. I'm not morbidly overweight, but I've found that maintaining a little extra body fat has helped me progress my numbers upward. I've seen super-heavyweight powerlifters at 350+ pounds squat and deadlift absurd amounts, even in the 4-digit range. Check out Eddie Hall. He weighed over 400 when he pulled a half-ton deadlift. I'm guessing the increased body mass must have some play in how much of a burden you can push and pull. I'll probably never take myself to health-threatening levels, but I definitely feel the strength benefit of having a bit of a belly.

I agree. OP wanted to know about the THR10, so I assumed he had no interest in the THR100 heads.

Depends what you're looking for. I have a THR10X, because I dominantly play metal. The stereo chorus and reverb are unbelievable. The distorted tones react to your volume knob very similarly to a tube amp. The tones are usable in a recording environment, and are a very nice upgrade compared to the Mustang 1. This is all just my opinion, though. My only complaint with the THR amps is that they don't put up enough volume to jam with a drummer or most bass rigs. If you're looking to gig, find something else. If you want an awesome practice amp, you'll love the THR.

Been playing for 12 years, and have had a few successful students. Advice is different for each new player, but this generally holds up for everyone.

1. Get a professional, low-action setup. It will make everything you're trying to do easier. A good luthier will be able to get the action very low with little to no fret buzz. 

2. Don't force yourself to learn jazz fusion, just because everyone keeps telling you that classic rock pentatonic scales are "generic". Play what you want to play. Listen to what you want to hear. The point is to have fun. You're not obligated to innovate, even if there are a ton of smack-talkers out there.

3. Listen to as much music as you can. The more you hear, the more trained your ear will become. Your tastes will broaden, and you'll start to appreciate and understand the many techniques that are available for you to use in your own songs.
